title: How do you conduct a training needs analysis?
seoTitle: How to conduct a training needs analysis
description: A seven step method for training needs analysis in regulated organizations: organization, task and person analysis, prioritization, and a TNA template.
shortAnswer: A training needs analysis (TNA) is conducted in seven steps: define the performance problem, confirm training is the right response, analyze the organization, analyze the tasks and required standard, analyze the people who do them, prioritize needs by risk and size of gap, and record a specification that states the audience, learning outcomes, delivery approach and how success will be measured.
keyTakeaways: Start from a performance problem or obligation, not from a request for a course. Many gaps are better fixed by process, tooling, supervision or hiring.
Analyze at three levels: the organization, the tasks and their required standard, and the individuals who perform them.
In regulated sectors the task standard often comes from the regulator. Rules as different as AML/CTF guidance and medicines manufacturing regulations expect training to be matched to role and risk.
Prioritize needs by consequence of failure multiplied by the size and spread of the gap, then fund from the top.
The output is a written specification that the design team, the budget holder and an auditor can all read.

sections.heading: What does a training needs analysis produce?

blocks.text: A training needs analysis produces a decision record: which performance gaps exist, which of them training can close, who needs what, in what order, and how the result will be judged. It is an input to design, not a design document itself.

The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) describes the core logic as knowing the organization's current and future capability needs and then assessing existing levels of skills, attitudes and knowledge, so that decisions can be made about learning at individual, team or organizational level ([CIPD](https://www.cipd.org/en/knowledge/factsheets/learning-needs-factsheet/)). CIPD also distinguishes an ongoing learning needs analysis from a TNA, which it describes as a one-off analysis for a specific training activity.

The three level structure used below (organization, task, person) traces back to McGehee and Thayer's 1961 work on training in business and industry and remains the standard frame. For the difference between this exercise and a comparison against a fixed standard, see [training needs analysis vs gap analysis](/compare/training-needs-analysis-vs-gap-analysis).

sections.heading: What are the steps in a training needs analysis?

blocks.text: There are seven steps. Each one produces a named output, and the analysis is complete only when all seven exist in writing.

items: **Define the trigger and the performance problem.** State what is happening, what should be happening, and the evidence for the difference: incident data, audit findings, complaint trends, a new obligation, a new product or system. Output: a one paragraph problem statement with its evidence sources.

**Test whether training is the right response.** Ask whether people could do the task correctly if their life depended on it. If yes, the cause is usually process, tools, incentives, workload or supervision, not knowledge or skill. The ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group lists hiring, on the job training, mentoring, reassigning tasks, adjusting the scope of a job and subcontracting as legitimate ways to acquire competence alongside training ([ISO and IAF](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176/files/PDF%20APG%20New%20Disclaimer%2012-2023/ISO-TC%20176-TF_APG-Competence.pdf)). Output: a cause analysis that splits the problem into a training component and a non-training component, each with an owner.

**Analyze the organization.** Identify the strategic, regulatory and risk context: which business units, products and obligations are affected, what is changing, and what resources and constraints apply. Output: a scope statement listing the business units, roles and obligations in scope.

**Analyze the tasks.** For each role in scope, list the critical tasks and the standard each must be performed to. Draw the standard from the most authoritative source available: regulator guidance, an internal procedure, a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework), or a national unit of competency. Output: a task and standard list per role.

**Analyze the people.** Establish who currently performs each task and how well, using performance data, quality review results, observation, knowledge checks, manager input and existing training records. Output: a population profile showing numbers of people, current proficiency and where the gap sits.

**Prioritize.** Rate each need on consequence (what happens if the task is done wrongly) and gap (how many people, how far below standard). Output: a ranked needs list with a cut line agreed with the budget holder.

**Specify.** For each need above the cut line, write the target audience, draft [learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes), preferred delivery approach, timing, assessment approach and the measure that will show the need has been met. Output: the TNA specification, signed off by the business owner.

sections.heading: Where do task standards come from in a regulated organization?

blocks.text: In a regulated organization the task standard in step 4 is often set, or at least framed, by the regulator. The analysis should cite that source directly so the resulting training can be traced back to it.

items: **Medicines manufacturers.** In the United States, current good manufacturing practice regulations require that "Training shall be in the particular operations that the employee performs" and in good manufacturing practice "as they relate to the employee's functions" ([21 CFR 211.25(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211/subpart-B/section-211.25)). Identifying those operations and functions for each role is a TNA in all but name.

**AML/CTF reporting entities.** In Australia, AUSTRAC guidance on the reformed regime says training must be tailored to the person, their role, their responsibilities and the money laundering and terrorism financing risks relevant to that role, and that AUSTRAC expects entities to use their risk assessment to identify training needs ([AUSTRAC](https://www.austrac.gov.au/about-us/amlctf-reform/reforms-guidance/amlctf-program-reform/personnel-due-diligence-and-training-reform/amlctf-training-reform)).

**Work health and safety.** Safe Work Australia guidance says the type and amount of training will vary by worker, and that the characteriztics of the workplace and the level of risk in the work must be considered ([guidance](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/safety-topic/managing-health-and-safety/training-and-supporting-your-workers-stay-safe-work)).

blocks.text: Where no regulator standard exists, use a documented internal standard and record who approved it. An analysis that cannot name its standard cannot show that its conclusions are correct.

sections.heading: Which data sources should a TNA use?

blocks.text: Use at least one source of evidence about actual performance and at least one about required performance. Opinion surveys alone describe what people want to learn, not what they need to learn.

blocks.caption: Evidence sources by level of analysis
head: Level
Evidence about required performance
Evidence about actual performance
rows: Organization
Strategy, risk register, obligations register, regulator guidance, audit scope
Audit and regulator findings, incident and breach data, complaint trends
Task
Procedures, work instructions, competency frameworks, units of competency, role descriptions
Quality assurance sampling, error rates, process metrics, observation of work
Person
Role profile and required proficiency level
Knowledge checks, supervisor assessment, prior training and assessment records, self assessment used with caution

sections.heading: What does a completed TNA record look like?

blocks.text: A completed TNA record is one row per need, with enough detail for a designer to start work and for a reviewer to see the reasoning. The example below is illustrative only: the organization, figures and findings are invented to show the format.

blocks.caption: Illustrative TNA record for a retail bank contact center
head: Field
Illustrative entry
rows: Problem statement
Quality sampling found escalations of unusual transactions were incomplete in a material share of reviewed calls over two quarters
Source of standard
Internal suspicious matter escalation procedure; AUSTRAC guidance that customer facing staff need awareness of suspicious indicators and reporting procedures
Cause analysis
Training component: staff could not name the indicators. Non-training component: the escalation form had no mandatory fields (owner: operations)
Roles and population
Contact center consultants (about 240) and team leaders (about 20)
Current proficiency
Knowledge check: most consultants identified fewer than half of the listed indicators
Priority
High: consequence is a reporting failure; gap is broad
Draft outcome
Given a recorded call scenario, identify each suspicious indicator present and complete an escalation that meets the procedure
Approach
Scenario based module, team leader coaching, form redesign
Success measure
Escalation completeness in quality sampling at or above the agreed threshold for two consecutive months

sections.heading: What are the common mistakes in a training needs analysis?

blocks.text: The most common mistake is treating the TNA as a survey of training requests. The second is skipping the cause analysis, which produces courses for problems training cannot fix.

items: Stopping at the organization level and never specifying tasks or standards.
Measuring need by completion records. The ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group notes that participation in a course alone does not necessarily show a person is competent.
Leaving out contractors and third parties who perform regulated tasks.
Writing outcomes as topics ('AML awareness') instead of observable performance.
No success measure, which makes later [training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness) reporting impossible.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records the obligations, roles, concepts and assessment points of a domain as a structured framework before content is written. A needs analysis can then be run against that framework, so each identified need is linked to the obligation and role it came from and to the outcome that will close it. See [gap analysis](/platform/gap-analysis) for how this works in practice.

faqs.q: How long does a training needs analysis take?
faqs.a: It depends on scope. A focused TNA for one role and one change can be completed in days if performance data is available. An organization wide analysis across many roles takes weeks, mostly spent collecting evidence of actual performance and agreeing task standards with subject matter experts and business owners.

faqs.q: Who should own a training needs analysis?
faqs.a: The business owner of the performance problem should own the decision, with L&D running the analysis. In regulated areas the compliance or risk function should confirm the task standards, because they are accountable for interpreting the obligation the training is meant to support.

faqs.q: Is a skills survey enough for a TNA?
faqs.a: No. Self reported skill levels are useful for engagement and for spotting perceived gaps, but people often misjudge their own proficiency. Combine surveys with objective evidence such as quality sampling, knowledge checks, observation and incident data before committing budget.

faqs.q: How often should a training needs analysis be repeated?
faqs.a: Repeat it when a trigger occurs: a new or changed obligation, a new product or system, a significant incident, or an audit finding. Many organizations also run an annual review. AUSTRAC, for example, expects training to be updated in response to law changes, new risks and compliance review findings.
